text: Last year I went camping with my cousins and we swam in a lake. I have never been to a concert, but I would love to go to one.
What is the past simple of “eat”?
Okay, listen. I have a dare for everyone. We all make a bucket list this term, and we tick it off before the break.
A bucket list is a list of things you want to do once in a lifetime.
Mine is ready. Number one: give surfing a go. I have never been in the ocean, but I have seen a hundred videos.
That is brave, Vee. I have been to the beach, but I have never tried surfing.
Last summer I went to Spain with my cousin. We ate pizza every day, and we took hundreds of photos.
Ava, you have flown across the world twice, and you say you are not brave?
Flying is easy, Theo. Falling off a surfboard is the scary part.
I have taken a photo in every country I have visited. That is my record.
So here is the dare: three things you have done, and three things you want to do. Who has gone the furthest? Who has eaten the strangest thing?
Wait. Have you ever eaten spicy noodles?
Ha! That is number two on my list.
Why does Ava say that flying is easy?
What can you guess about Theo?

A bucket list is a list of things you want to do in your life. A dare is when someone asks you to do something scary. To give it a go means to try. Once in a lifetime happens only one time. To tick it off is to mark it as done. Brave means not afraid when something is hard.
Say them with me: bucket list, dare, give it a go, once in a lifetime, tick it off, brave.
What is the main idea of Ava’s post?
How did Ava probably feel when her cousin first dared her?
Is the time finished and stated, or is it an experience up to now?
Every verb has three forms: base, past simple, past participle. go, went, gone
Past simple: a finished time, so we say when. I went to Spain last summer.
Have and the past participle: an experience up to now, no time. I have been to Spain.
Have you ever been to Japan

Welcome to the Travel Club! Look at the postcard wall. Everyone sent a postcard from a bucket-list trip.
But I need the right words for every postcard. “Good” and “nice” are not enough!
My postcard is from the countryside. We stayed there for a weekend, and I felt so relaxed.
The view was amazing, and I was grateful that my cousin invited me.
Mine is from a big city. We went sightseeing, and my favorite attraction was an old tower.
At the top I was a little frightened, but I was proud that I did it.
I went camping with my family. I was embarrassed because I forgot my sleeping bag!
But I was proud when I finished the hike, and I would love to try something new every year.
Perfect. Where was your destination? What did you do? How did you feel? Let’s find the words.
Where did Ava go for her weekend?
What did Theo do in the city?
excitement. a strong, happy feeling before something good. The excitement before my trip kept me awake.
amazed. very surprised, in a good way. I was amazed when I saw the mountains.
disappointed. sad because something was not as good as you hoped. We were disappointed when the museum was closed.
embarrassed. shy and uncomfortable because of something that happened. I was embarrassed when I dropped my tray.
proud. happy about something you did, or about someone you care about. I was proud when I finished the hike.
frightened. afraid. I was frightened at the top of the tower.
relaxed. calm and comfortable, not worried. I felt relaxed in the countryside.
grateful. thankful for something good that someone did. I am grateful to my friends for the trip.
destination. the place you are going to. Our destination was a small village.
attraction. a place that people visit for fun or interest. The tower is the city’s best attraction.
Is it a person who feels it, or a thing that makes you feel it?
We went camping near a lake. I felt relaxed, and the view was amazing. Our destination was a small village.
Say it with me: I felt relaxed. The view was amazing. Our destination was a small village.
Words like amazed, proud and frightened say how a person feels. I felt amazed.
Go camping, go sightseeing and try something new are whole chunks: learn each one as one piece. We went camping. I have been sightseeing in Rome.
A destination is where you are going; an attraction is a place to visit; the countryside is land outside the city. Our destination was the countryside.
countryside. land outside towns and cities, with fields and nature. We spent the weekend in the countryside.
go camping. to sleep outside for a night or more, for fun. We went camping near a lake.
go sightseeing. to visit famous places in a town or city. We went sightseeing in Rome.
try something new. to do something for the first time. I want to try something new this summer.
We went camping near the lake
They went sightseeing in the city
I want to try something new this summer

Three steps: the place, what you did, how you felt. Say it with me: It was our destination. We went camping. I felt relaxed.
My postcard is from the countryside. It was our destination. We went camping and I felt relaxed because it was quiet.
I have been to the countryside, and I felt so relaxed. Our destination was a small village. I went last August, and I was proud because I tried something new.

Watch me. I have the parts: have, never, been, to, Lisbon. I have never been to Lisbon. Now a question: Have you ever been to Rome? Yes, I have. I went last summer, with my family.
First the experience with have. Then the details, when and where, in the past simple. Say it with me: Have you ever been to Rome? Yes, I have.
Have or has and a past participle tell an experience up to now, with no finished time. I have flown. She has never eaten sushi.
Never means not once. Ever, in a question, means at any time in your life. Have you ever flown in a plane? Yes, I have. No, I haven’t.
Been means went and came back. Gone means went and is still there. For the details, when and where, use the past simple. I have been to Lisbon. I went last summer.
I have been to Rome twice
He has gone to the library

Theo, have you ever been to Lisbon? … No, never. I have been to Rome twice. … Have you ever been to Portugal? … Hmm. Once. … When did you go? … I went last summer. … Aha! You said never, but you went last summer!
You found the contradiction with a question and a follow-up. Say the two questions with me: Have you ever been to Portugal? When did you go?
I have never been to Lisbon. I have been to Rome twice.
Hmm. Once. A long time ago.
Once. A long time ago. It was nothing special.
I went last summer. With my family.
I went last summer. With my family. But I have never taken a postcard!
Okay, okay. I took the postcard to copy the stamp. I am sorry, Vee!
Have you ever flown in a plane? Yes, I have. When did you fly? I flew last year.
Have you ever eaten snails? Yes, I have. When did you eat them? I ate them in France, two years ago.
I have never flown in a plane. I have been to the mountains twice. I went last winter. Have you ever been to the mountains?
Have and a participle tell an experience up to now. When do we use the past simple instead?

Last month my cousin dared me to write a bucket list, and I laughed. Honestly, I thought bucket lists were only for grown-ups.

Then I counted what I have already done. I have flown across the world twice, I have slept in a tent in the rain, and I have eaten insects in Thailand. Last summer I went to Spain, and I even gave paragliding a go.

The strange thing is that I have never felt brave. Brave people are not afraid, I used to think, but I was terrified before every one of those things. Now I believe it is the opposite: you are brave when you do it anyway.
So this term I am going to tick off three more things, and one of them is a once in a lifetime trip. I have never tried surfing, and I have never performed on a stage.
If you have a dare for yourself, write it down. You will probably regret the things you did not try more than the things you did.
